A carbohydrate chain can take 3 forms: simple, complex, fibrous. Imagine braiding a simple thread with others to make a thicker rope.

Simple Carbs are what we call sugar... quick energy burn, and gone, the body uses these for primary sources of energy.

Complex Carbs are what we call starches... the energy burn lasts a bit longer, which is why they are recommended for athletes and such for endurance energy. Also why "standard diets" make them a staple.

Fibrous Carbs are what we call fiber... at this point the rope is so thick we can't use it... the body dispels this as waste material. (Fiber makes you poop.)

The point is, on nutrition labels all 3 are combined in the Total Carbohydrate Nutrition column. As we cannot digest the fiber we do not count it in the Net Carbohydrate count.

If you use a popular food tracking app, set your macros accordingly and check your nutrition count, you see your total carbs, and you see your fiber consumed... Try to make sure any extra carbs you use are less than or equal to fiber consumed.

I moved many datasets between aggregates on a system this way; it can be fairly convoluted, but it does work well. Now to your questions.

1. Mirroring the storage tree does work, but will require some temporary downtime, as you will likely want to perform a snapshot mirror of the storage tree to transfer a majority of the data, shut down the virtual machine, so you get the data in a static state, and update the snapshot mirror once more once this is done.

2. The old volume will remain where it is and writable, which is why it's very important it's unmounted from the host when you do the final sync-up snapshot mirror to ensure there is no change of data in the source volume.

3. If you rename the old volume to volume_old and rename your volume_mirror to volume, you will still need to reconnect to it. As I stated before, ideally you will want to have this unmounted and inaccessible for a short time to complete a final sync.

Vol move is your best bet for uninterrupted data moves, but the method you described with a data replication tool would work too, and would be the only way to do it with remote legacy storage systems.
